items.q: A dialysis-dependent patient has severe persistent hyperphosphatemia despite dietary restriction and binders. Which removal method does the page call the best?
items.exp: Dialysis is listed as the best removal method in this context, alongside intake restriction and attention to associated hypocalcemia. (Book p890)

items.q: Which proposed diet change conflicts with the chapter's hyperphosphatemia advice?
items.exp: The restriction list includes dairy products, pickles, nuts, chocolate and dates; increasing dairy and nuts goes against it. (Book p890)

items.q: Assess: I Management includes attention to associated hypocalcemia. II Every asymptomatic low calcium during phosphate excess requires aggressive calcium loading.
items.exp: The page says to treat associated hypocalcemia, but aggressive calcium loading can increase calcium–phosphate precipitation; severity and symptoms guide clinical treatment. (Book p890)

items.q: The clinical-feature list for severe hypophosphatemia is introduced at serum phosphate below ___ mg/dL.
items.exp: The page associates clinically significant depletion with phosphate <1 mg/dL. (Book p890)

items.q: Match the following depletion effects — 1) RBC 2) Cardiac muscle 3) Proximal skeletal muscle … A) Hemolysis B) Myopathy C) Cardiomyopathy
items.exp: The feature list includes RBC hemolysis, cardiomyopathy and proximal myopathy, as well as growth retardation and rhabdomyolysis. (Book p890)

items.q: Which is the odd one out among the listed severe phosphate-depletion consequences?
items.exp: Calcific masses belong to phosphate excess/tumoral calcinosis, unlike the depletion features listed here. (Book p890)

items.q: A malnourished patient with phosphate 0.6 mg/dL develops rhabdomyolysis; phosphate then rises as muscle breaks down. Which explanation reconciles this sequence?
opts: Depletion predisposes to injury; cell lysis subsequently releases phosphate
Rhabdomyolysis can only occur after phosphate excess
The initial low value rules out a causal role for depletion
Both measurements must be laboratory errors
items.exp: The note explicitly distinguishes low phosphate as a risk factor from high phosphate resulting from muscle-cell release after rhabdomyolysis. (Book p890)

items.q: Evaluate the source's vitamin-D note: I Severe deficiency can lower phosphate. II Every mild vitamin-D deficiency must produce severe phosphate depletion.
items.exp: The note emphasizes severe vitamin-D deficiency and severe hypocalcemia, rather than claiming that all lesser deficiencies cause profound hypophosphatemia. (Book p890)

items.q: During treatment of DKA, phosphate falls after insulin begins. Which mechanism best fits?
items.exp: Insulin after DKA is listed among blood-to-cell redistribution causes; this differs from cellular destruction. (Book p890)

items.q: The most characteristic metabolic abnormality named for refeeding syndrome is ___.
items.exp: The page identifies low phosphate as the most common metabolic abnormality of refeeding. (Book p890)

items.q: Match the following low-phosphate mechanisms — 1) Nutritional rickets 2) Refeeding 3) Hungry bone syndrome … A) Insulin-associated intracellular shift B) Increased skeletal mineral uptake C) Reduced nutrient/vitamin-D supply
items.exp: The source separates reduced intake from redistribution; hungry bone directs minerals into bone, while refeeding drives cellular uptake. (Book p890)

items.q: Which does not belong in the page's hypophosphatemic redistribution list?
items.exp: Sepsis, heat stroke and hyperthermia are listed with redistribution causes; FGF23 loss impairs phosphate excretion and favors hyperphosphatemia. (Book p890)

items.q: In the sepsis note, evaluate: I The phosphate fall is emphasized more than the calcium fall. II The shorthand excludes coexisting hypophosphatemia.
items.exp: The shorthand is '↓Ca > ↓P': a relative emphasis, not exclusion of hypophosphatemia. (Book p890)
